title: When a Reader Blocks a Writer (HOLDLOCK)
description: A HOLDLOCK reader keeps its shared lock and blocks a writer; drop the hint (or use snapshot) so the read doesn't hold locks. Why it matters: "readers block writers" reverses the usual assumption and is a common source of confusing incidents when a report or dashboard query holds locks longer than expected.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Most people, once they understand ordinary locking, walk away with the takeaway "writers block readers" — a writer holds an exclusive lock, and a reader waiting behind it has to wait its turn, as covered in the very first lesson of this level. This lesson is about the surprising exception: a specific, deliberate hint that flips that expectation around and makes a *reader* block a *writer* instead — the reverse of what most people assume is even possible.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** This lesson is about the `HOLDLOCK` hint (which is equivalent to running under the SERIALIZABLE isolation level for that specific query) applied to a plain `SELECT`, and about how it changes an ordinary, seemingly harmless read into something that actively blocks a completely unrelated writer trying to modify the same rows.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Under the ordinary default isolation behavior covered earlier in this course, a plain `SELECT` takes a shared lock on the rows it reads, but releases that lock essentially immediately once it's done reading each row — it doesn't hold onto it for the rest of the transaction. That's exactly why a quick, simple `SELECT` doesn't normally cause any lasting trouble for other sessions. But some code, often written by someone trying to be extra careful about consistency, deliberately adds a `HOLDLOCK` (or `WITH (SERIALIZABLE)`) hint to a read, specifically to guarantee something stronger: "make sure the rows I'm reading right now don't change at all until my entire transaction is completely finished." That's a legitimate thing to want in certain situations — but it fundamentally changes what the read leaves behind.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** With `HOLDLOCK` applied, the `SELECT`'s shared lock is no longer released right after each row is read — it's held for the rest of the enclosing transaction, exactly the way an ordinary writer's exclusive lock is held, just with a shared lock instead of an exclusive one. If that read's transaction then goes on to do other, possibly slow, work before eventually committing — call an external service, wait on some other condition, run additional queries — that shared lock sits there the whole time, just like an uncommitted writer's exclusive lock would in the very first lesson of this course, except now it's a reader holding it. Now suppose a completely different session comes along and tries to `UPDATE` one of those same rows. An `UPDATE` needs an exclusive lock, and an exclusive lock is incompatible with any shared lock still being held — including this long-held one from the `HOLDLOCK` read. The writer blocks, waiting for the reader's entire transaction to finish and finally release that shared lock — the exact mirror image of the very first lesson's reader-blocks-behind-a-writer scenario, just with the roles of reader and writer swapped.

**Why this matters in production.** "Readers block writers" reverses the usual assumption most developers carry after learning about basic locking, and it's genuinely counterintuitive precisely because it contradicts what people learn first — that reads are supposed to be the safe, harmless, "just looking" operation that doesn't hold anything up. When `HOLDLOCK` (or an equivalent stronger isolation level) is applied somewhere in a codebase, often for a legitimate-sounding reason like "I need to make sure this data doesn't change out from under my report while I'm generating it," it introduces exactly this reversed blocking risk, and if that reading transaction happens to run for a while — again, waiting on something slow, or simply doing more work before committing — every writer trying to touch those same rows is stuck waiting the whole time, producing symptoms that look identical to the classic blocking scenario, except that this time, staring at the query that's "just reading" as the culprit feels wrong to whoever's investigating, because reads "aren't supposed to" hold things up.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is recognizing when that strong a guarantee is actually necessary, and when it isn't: if the read doesn't genuinely need the rows to stay frozen for the rest of its own transaction, dropping the `HOLDLOCK` hint entirely restores the ordinary, quick-release shared-lock behavior and removes the blocking risk. And if some stronger consistency guarantee genuinely is needed, an alternative like SNAPSHOT isolation (covered elsewhere in this course) can often deliver a consistent view of the data via row versioning instead of long-held locks — giving the reader the stability it needs without holding a lock that blocks anyone else at all.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below has a session read a row with `HOLDLOCK` and then pause before committing, and shows you a completely separate writer blocking behind that held shared lock — the mirror image of the very first lesson in this level. After removing the `HOLDLOCK` hint, re-run the same interleaving and watch the writer proceed immediately, no longer stuck waiting behind a read that no longer holds its lock past the moment it finished reading.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** `HOLDLOCK` is sometimes added defensively by developers who read about phantom reads or dirty reads and want to "be safe," without fully weighing the concurrency cost of holding shared locks for an entire transaction's duration. Before reaching for `HOLDLOCK` (or SERIALIZABLE generally), it's worth asking specifically what guarantee the code actually needs — RCSI or plain SNAPSHOT isolation (covered elsewhere in this course) can often deliver a stable, consistent view of the data via row versioning without holding any lock that would block a concurrent writer at all, which is usually the better default unless the code genuinely needs to block writers from changing rows currently being examined.

It's worth treating any occurrence of `HOLDLOCK`, `WITH (SERIALIZABLE)`, or an explicit `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE` on a read-only query as something to double check during code review, specifically asking whether the guarantee it provides is actually required by the logic that follows, and whether the transaction holding it could be made shorter regardless, since a shorter hold time shrinks the blocking window even when the strong isolation level itself is genuinely necessary.

## Scenario
We usually say "writers block readers." Here it's the reverse: a long-running read report (Session A) holds Alice's row with a **`HOLDLOCK`** hint while it finishes, and a simple `UPDATE` (Session B) on that row hangs until the report commits. The report only *reads* — yet it stalls every write to the row.

## Why it blocks
`HOLDLOCK` (a synonym for `SERIALIZABLE` at the statement level) tells SQL Server to **keep the shared (S) lock** A takes on Alice's row until A's transaction commits — instead of releasing it the instant the read finishes (the default `READ COMMITTED` behavior). B's `UPDATE` needs an **exclusive (X)** lock, which is incompatible with A's still-held S lock, so B waits for A's whole transaction.

## What to look for
- A takes an **S** lock and holds it; B blocks requesting **X** on the same row.
- The culprit is the `HOLDLOCK` hint (or a session-wide `REPEATABLE READ`/`SERIALIZABLE` setting), not an uncommitted write.

## The concept
Don't hold read locks longer than you need. Removing `HOLDLOCK` lets A's shared lock drop as soon as the row is read, so B's update proceeds immediately. If the report genuinely needs a stable view, use **`SNAPSHOT`**/RCSI row-versioning instead — it gives consistent reads with **no** shared locks, so it never blocks writers.
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Stop Session A's read from holding its shared lock, then Run the interleaving.
hints: Session A only reads, but it keeps its shared lock until commit. What on A's SELECT forces that?
HOLDLOCK = SERIALIZABLE for that statement: the S lock is held to the end of the transaction, blocking B's X lock.
Remove the WITH (HOLDLOCK) hint so the S lock releases right after the read (or switch A to SNAPSHOT for a lock-free consistent read).

interleaving.description: Session A holds a shared lock on Alice's row via HOLDLOCK; Session B's UPDATE of that row blocks behind the held S lock.

A.sql: BEGIN TRAN; SELECT AccountId, Owner, Balance FROM Accounts WITH (HOLDLOCK) WHERE AccountId = 1;

B.sql: UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 50 WHERE AccountId = 1;

interleaving.solutionNote: Remove the WITH (HOLDLOCK) hint so A's shared lock is released as soon as the row is read (default READ COMMITTED), letting B's UPDATE proceed. If A needs a stable read, use SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT (row versioning) instead, which takes no shared locks and so never blocks the writer.
